questions.questionText: Who originally created the Linux kernel in 1991?

explanation.correct: Linus Torvalds, a Finnish student, released the first version of the Linux kernel in 1991.
explanation.incorrect: Stallman founded the GNU Project and FSF; Ritchie co-created Unix and C; Shuttleworth founded Ubuntu/Canonical.
explanation.examTip: Remember: Linus Torvalds = kernel, Richard Stallman = GNU userland tools. Together they form 'GNU/Linux'.

metadata.examObjective: 1.1 Linux Evolution and Popular Operating Systems

questions.questionText: Under which license is the Linux kernel primarily distributed?

explanation.correct: The Linux kernel is licensed under the GNU General Public License version 2 (GPLv2), a copyleft license.
explanation.incorrect: MIT, Apache, and BSD are permissive licenses that do not require derivative works to stay open source; the kernel uses copyleft GPLv2 instead.
explanation.examTip: GPL = copyleft, must share source of derivatives. MIT/BSD = permissive, can be closed-sourced.

questions.questionText: Which package manager is used natively by Fedora and Red Hat Enterprise Linux?

explanation.correct: Fedora and RHEL use dnf (the successor to yum) to manage RPM packages.
explanation.incorrect: apt is Debian/Ubuntu's manager, pacman is Arch Linux's manager, and zypper is used by openSUSE/SUSE.
explanation.examTip: Match the family: Debian/Ubuntu=apt, Fedora/RHEL=dnf, Arch=pacman, SUSE=zypper.

questions.questionText: Which organization, founded by Richard Stallman, promotes the philosophy of free software?

explanation.correct: Richard Stallman founded the Free Software Foundation (FSF) in 1985 to promote free software and launched the GNU Project.
explanation.incorrect: The Linux Foundation supports kernel development and industry collaboration; the Apache Software Foundation and OSI are separate organizations with different missions.
explanation.examTip: FSF = Stallman, 'free as in freedom.' GNU = 'GNU's Not Unix,' the FSF's operating system project.

metadata.examObjective: 1.1 Linux Evolution and Popular Operating Systems

questions.questionText: Which TWO of the following are considered copyleft open source licenses?

explanation.correct: GPL and LGPL are copyleft licenses: derivative works must also be distributed under the same or compatible license terms.
explanation.incorrect: The MIT and BSD licenses are permissive licenses; they allow derivative works to be relicensed, including as proprietary software.
explanation.examTip: Copyleft 'shares alike'; permissive lets you do almost anything, including closing the source.

questions.questionText: Which TWO of the following distributions are based on Debian?

explanation.correct: Ubuntu and Linux Mint are both derived from Debian and use the apt/dpkg package management system.
explanation.incorrect: Fedora is an independent, Red Hat-sponsored distribution using dnf/rpm, and openSUSE uses zypper/rpm.
explanation.examTip: Debian family uses .deb packages and apt; Red Hat/SUSE families use .rpm packages.

metadata.examObjective: 1.1 Linux Evolution and Popular Operating Systems

questions.questionText: Evaluate each statement about Linux and open source concepts as Yes or No.

explanation.correct: GNU/Linux correctly describes kernel+userland; a distribution bundles the kernel with a package manager, utilities, and often a desktop environment, so it is not the same as the kernel alone; Apache and Nginx are indeed both open source web servers.
explanation.incorrect: The kernel is only the core of the operating system, not the whole distribution.
explanation.examTip: Kernel = engine. Distribution = whole car (engine + body + wheels + software).

statements.text: The term 'GNU/Linux' reflects that a typical Linux distribution combines the Linux kernel with GNU userland utilities.
A Linux 'distribution' is identical to the Linux 'kernel' and the two terms are interchangeable.
Apache HTTP Server and Nginx are both examples of open source web server software.

questions.questionText: Evaluate each statement about Linux in cloud and DevOps environments as Yes or No.

explanation.correct: Containers share the host kernel (that's what makes them lightweight compared to VMs); all major cloud providers offer Linux VM images; server distributions frequently ship with no GUI at all.
explanation.incorrect: Many Linux servers, including most cloud and container images, are headless and run without any desktop environment.
explanation.examTip: Containers vs VMs: containers share the host kernel; VMs each run a full separate kernel via a hypervisor.

statements.text: Docker containers running on a Linux host share that host's kernel rather than each running their own full kernel.
AWS, Azure, and GCP offer Linux as one of the operating system choices for their virtual machine instances.
A Linux distribution is required to include a graphical desktop environment in order to be a valid distribution.

questions.questionText: Complete each statement by choosing the correct term from its dropdown.

explanation.correct: dnf is the modern RPM package manager for Fedora/RHEL, and Ubuntu is Canonical's flagship Debian-based distribution.
explanation.incorrect: apt belongs to Debian/Ubuntu, pacman to Arch, and zypper to SUSE — mixing these up is a common exam trap.
explanation.examTip: Associate each company/community with its distro: Canonical=Ubuntu, Red Hat=Fedora/RHEL, SUSE=openSUSE.

questions.questionText: Arrange the typical steps of contributing a code change to an open source project on a site like GitHub in the correct order.

explanation.correct: This is the standard open source contribution workflow: fork, clone, commit locally, then submit a pull request for review.
explanation.incorrect: Skipping the fork step (working directly on the original repo) or opening a pull request before pushing changes would not work in this workflow.
explanation.examTip: Fork-Clone-Commit-Pull request — the classic four-step open source contribution cycle.

orderItems.text: Fork the project's repository into your own account
Clone your fork to your local machine
Make and commit your code changes locally
Push the changes and open a pull request against the original project

questions.questionText: Sort each software license into the correct licensing category.

explanation.correct: GPL and LGPL require derivative works to remain under compatible open terms (copyleft), while MIT and BSD allow much more freedom, including closed-source derivatives (permissive).
explanation.incorrect: A common mistake is treating LGPL as permissive — it is still copyleft, just with weaker linking restrictions than GPL.
explanation.examTip: Copyleft = 'share alike'; Permissive = 'do almost anything.'

questions.questionText: Which directory in the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS) contains system-wide configuration files?

explanation.correct: /etc contains host-specific system configuration files, such as /etc/passwd and /etc/fstab.
explanation.incorrect: /var holds variable data like logs, /opt holds optional third-party software, and /tmp holds temporary files that may be cleared on reboot.
explanation.examTip: '/etc' has no acronym — think 'et cetera,' the catch-all for config files.

questions.questionText: Which command prints the current working directory?

explanation.correct: pwd stands for 'print working directory' and outputs the full absolute path of the current directory.
explanation.incorrect: ls lists directory contents, cd changes the directory, and dir is not a standard Linux command (it exists on Windows).
explanation.examTip: pwd = Print Working Directory — one of the very first commands most people learn.

questions.questionText: Which ls option sorts output by modification time, showing the most recently modified files first?

explanation.correct: ls -t sorts files by modification time, newest first.
explanation.incorrect: -S sorts by file size, -R lists recursively through subdirectories, and -h only makes sizes human-readable when combined with -l.
explanation.examTip: -t = Time, -S = Size, -R = Recursive, -h = Human-readable (needs -l to matter).

questions.questionText: In a path, what does a single dot (.) represent?

explanation.correct: A single dot (.) always refers to the current working directory.
explanation.incorrect: The parent directory is represented by two dots (..), the home directory by ~, and the root directory by a leading /.
explanation.examTip: . = here, .. = one level up, ~ = home. Easy to mix up under exam pressure.

questions.scenarioText: A developer at Umbrella Corp is scaffolding a new project and wants to build out a nested folder structure in one command.
questions.questionText: Which command creates a directory along with any missing parent directories in one step?

explanation.correct: mkdir -p creates the full path, including any parent directories that do not yet exist, without raising an error if they already do.
explanation.incorrect: -r is not a valid mkdir flag, --all does not exist for mkdir, and touch creates files rather than directories.
explanation.examTip: -p in mkdir = 'parents' (create the whole path); the same -p in cp means 'preserve attributes' — don't confuse them.

questions.questionText: Which command searches the filesystem in real time for files modified within the last 2 days?

explanation.correct: find searches the live filesystem, and -mtime -2 matches files modified less than 2 days ago.
explanation.incorrect: locate does not support -mtime (it only searches its prebuilt database by name); -atime matches access time, not modification time; which only locates executables in $PATH.
explanation.examTip: find searches live and supports -mtime/-size/-type; locate is a fast name-only search of a prebuilt database.

questions.questionText: Which command tells you the full path of the executable that would run for a given command name, based on $PATH?

explanation.correct: which searches the directories listed in $PATH and reports the path of the executable that would be run.
explanation.incorrect: file identifies a file's type, stat shows detailed metadata about a file, and locate searches a filename database rather than $PATH.
explanation.examTip: which = 'which executable will run,' searched only within $PATH.

questions.questionText: Which command displays only the first 10 lines of a text file by default?

explanation.correct: head displays the beginning of a file, defaulting to the first 10 lines.
explanation.incorrect: tail shows the last 10 lines by default, more pages through the entire file, and wc counts lines/words/characters rather than displaying content.
explanation.examTip: head = top of file, tail = bottom of file. Use -n to change the line count for either.

questions.questionText: Which command removes duplicate adjacent lines from sorted input?

explanation.correct: uniq filters out repeated adjacent lines, which is why it is almost always used after sort to catch all duplicates.
explanation.incorrect: sort only orders lines (it does not remove duplicates by itself unless combined with uniq via sort -u), cut extracts columns/fields, and tr translates or deletes characters.
explanation.examTip: uniq only removes ADJACENT duplicates — always pipe through sort first: sort file | uniq.

questions.questionText: Which TWO commands can be used to display the contents of a text file directly in the terminal?

explanation.correct: cat prints an entire file to the terminal, and less pages through file content interactively.
explanation.incorrect: find searches for files by criteria (it does not display file contents), and mkdir creates directories.
explanation.examTip: Content viewers: cat, less, more, head, tail. Search tools: find, locate.

questions.questionText: Which TWO ls options, when combined, list all files (including hidden ones) with detailed, human-readable file sizes?

explanation.correct: -a shows hidden (dotfile) entries, and -h (used with -l) shows file sizes in human-readable units like K, M, and G.
explanation.incorrect: -R recurses into subdirectories, which is unrelated to hidden files or size formatting, and -x is not a standard ls option for this purpose.
explanation.examTip: ls -lah is one of the most common combos: long format + all files + human-readable sizes.

questions.questionText: Which TWO of the following are absolute paths?

explanation.correct: An absolute path always starts from the root directory (/), such as /home/frederick/notes.txt and /var/log/syslog.
explanation.incorrect: ../shared/notes.txt and ./notes.txt are relative paths because they are interpreted starting from the current working directory.
explanation.examTip: Absolute paths start with /. Relative paths start with . , .. , or a bare name, and depend on your current location.

questions.questionText: Which TWO find predicates can be used together to search for regular files larger than 100MB?

explanation.correct: -type f restricts the search to regular files, and -size +100M matches files larger than 100 megabytes.
explanation.incorrect: -type d matches directories, not files, and -size -100M would match files smaller than 100MB, the opposite of what's needed.
explanation.examTip: find -size uses + for 'greater than' and - for 'less than'; no sign means exact size.

questions.questionText: Evaluate each statement about find and locate as Yes or No.

explanation.correct: locate is fast because it queries an index built by updatedb rather than scanning disk; that index is only refreshed periodically (or manually via updatedb), so very recent files may be missing; find supports rich criteria beyond filenames, including -perm, -size, and -mtime.
explanation.incorrect: locate's database is not real-time — a file created moments ago may not appear until updatedb runs again.
explanation.examTip: find searches live (slow but current); locate searches an index (fast but can be stale) — run 'sudo updatedb' to refresh it.

statements.text: locate searches a prebuilt database and is generally faster than find for simple name searches.
locate always reflects files created in the last few seconds, with no need to update its database.
find can search based on file permissions, size, and modification time, not just filename.

questions.questionText: Evaluate each statement about navigating the filesystem as Yes or No.

explanation.correct: 'cd ..' moves to the parent; ~ represents the current user's HOME directory, not the filesystem root; relative paths are indeed resolved relative to wherever you currently are.
explanation.incorrect: Confusing ~ (home directory) with / (root directory) is a common beginner mistake.
explanation.examTip: ~ = $HOME (e.g. /home/frederick), / = filesystem root. Very different locations!

statements.text: The command 'cd ..' moves you up one directory level to the parent directory.
The tilde (~) character, when used alone, represents the root directory (/).
Relative paths are always interpreted based on the current working directory.

questions.questionText: Evaluate each statement about file and directory management commands as Yes or No.

explanation.correct: rm -r recurses into and deletes directory trees; rmdir only removes empty directories and fails on non-empty ones; touch either updates the access/modification timestamp of an existing file or creates a new empty file.
explanation.incorrect: To remove a non-empty directory you need rm -r (or rm -rf), not plain rmdir.
explanation.examTip: rmdir = empty directories only. rm -r = directories with contents. rm -rf = no confirmation, be careful!

statements.text: rm -r deletes a directory and all of its contents recursively.
rmdir can remove a non-empty directory without any additional flags.
touch updates a file's timestamp, or creates an empty file if it does not already exist.

questions.questionText: Complete each statement by choosing the correct command from its dropdown.

explanation.correct: tail -f follows a file and prints new lines as they are appended, ideal for watching logs live; wc -l counts the number of lines in a file.
explanation.incorrect: head shows the beginning of a file rather than following it, and sort/uniq/cut manipulate or reorder content rather than counting lines.
explanation.examTip: -f in 'tail -f' stands for 'follow' — extremely common for live log monitoring.

questions.questionText: Complete each statement about the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard by choosing the correct directory.

explanation.correct: /home holds regular users' personal directories, while /media is the traditional mount point for removable media like USB drives and CDs.
explanation.incorrect: /usr holds shared program files (not personal data), /root is specifically the superuser's home (not general users), and /proc is a virtual filesystem exposing kernel/process info.
explanation.examTip: /root is the root USER's home, completely separate from the / root DIRECTORY — a favorite exam trick.

questions.questionText: Complete each statement by choosing the correct command from its dropdown.

explanation.correct: cp -r recursively copies directories and their contents, and mv renames or moves files (renaming is just a move within the same directory).
explanation.incorrect: mv does not create a second copy (cp does), and ln creates a link rather than renaming a file.
explanation.examTip: mv does double duty: rename in place, or move to a new location — same command, same behavior.

questions.scenarioText: A junior developer at Initech is setting up a new Node.js project and needs to prepare the initial folder structure.
questions.questionText: A new engineer needs to create a nested project directory, move into it, and create a starter file. Arrange the commands in the correct order.

explanation.correct: You must first create the nested directories with mkdir -p, then cd into the new location, then create the file with touch, and finally verify it with ls -l.
explanation.incorrect: Running touch or cd before the directory exists would fail with a 'No such file or directory' error.
explanation.examTip: Create first, navigate second, act third, verify last — a pattern that applies to most filesystem workflows.

orderItems.text: mkdir -p ~/projects/webapp/src
cd ~/projects/webapp/src
touch index.js
ls -l

questions.questionText: Arrange the steps to locate the most recently modified log file in /var/log and view only its first 5 lines.

explanation.correct: ls -t sorts files newest-first, so the top entry is the most recently modified file; head -n 5 then shows only its first 5 lines.
explanation.incorrect: Running head before identifying the correct filename, or sorting with -S (size) instead of -t (time), would not answer the question correctly.
explanation.examTip: ls -t = newest first, ls -S = largest first. Don't mix these two flags up under time pressure.

orderItems.text: cd /var/log
ls -t
identify the file listed at the top of the output
run head -n 5 on that filename

questions.questionText: Sort each path into the correct category.

explanation.correct: Absolute paths begin with a leading slash and start from the filesystem root; relative paths begin with . , .. , or a bare name and are resolved from the current directory.
explanation.incorrect: Any path lacking a leading slash is relative, regardless of how many directories it traverses.
explanation.examTip: Quick test: does the path start with /? If yes, it's absolute — if no, it's relative.

questions.questionText: Sort each command into the category describing its primary purpose.

explanation.correct: find and locate are used to search the filesystem for files matching criteria, while cat and less are used to view the contents of files that have already been located.
explanation.incorrect: cat and less do not search for files; they display content once you already know the path.
explanation.examTip: Search first (find/locate), then view (cat/less/head/tail) — two separate stages of working with files.

questions.questionText: Sort each FHS directory into the category describing what it primarily stores.

explanation.correct: /etc and /var hold system configuration and variable system data respectively, while /home and /tmp are areas regular users routinely read and write to.
explanation.incorrect: While /tmp is technically system-managed, it is world-writable and used directly by ordinary users and applications, unlike /etc which regular users typically only read.
explanation.examTip: /etc = config, /var = logs & spool data, /home = personal files, /tmp = scratch space cleared periodically.

questions.questionText: Sort each ls -l flag into the category describing what it changes about the output.

explanation.correct: -t and -S both re-order the listing (by time or by size), while -a reveals additional hidden entries and -R adds recursive subdirectory listings — these affect content shown, not order.
explanation.incorrect: -a and -R do not change sort order; they change the scope/visibility of what ls reports.
explanation.examTip: Sorting flags (-t, -S, -X) vs. content flags (-a, -R, -l) serve different purposes — know which category each belongs to.

questions.questionText: Which environment variable holds the list of directories the shell searches for executable commands?

explanation.correct: $PATH contains a colon-separated list of directories the shell searches, in order, when you type a command name.
explanation.incorrect: $HOME holds the current user's home directory, $SHELL holds the path to the user's default shell, and $USER holds the current username.
explanation.examTip: Command not found? Check $PATH first — the shell can only find executables listed in it.

metadata.examObjective: 3.2 Using the Command Line to Get Help

questions.questionText: Which command permanently exports a variable so that it is inherited by child processes for the current session?

explanation.correct: export marks a shell variable as an environment variable, making it available to child processes spawned from that shell.
explanation.incorrect: set only lists or sets shell (not necessarily environment) variables, env displays or runs a command with a modified environment (it doesn't persist a variable in the current shell), and unset removes a variable entirely.
explanation.examTip: A shell variable becomes an 'environment' variable only after export — until then, child processes can't see it.

metadata.examObjective: 3.2 Using the Command Line to Get Help

questions.questionText: Which shell configuration file is read for non-login interactive bash shells, such as when opening a new terminal window?

explanation.correct: .bashrc is sourced for interactive non-login shells, such as a new terminal window in a graphical desktop.
explanation.incorrect: .bash_profile and /etc/profile are read for login shells, and .bash_login is an older, less commonly used login-shell file.
explanation.examTip: Login shell -> .bash_profile/.profile. Interactive non-login shell (new terminal tab) -> .bashrc.

questions.questionText: What does the redirection operator '2>&1' accomplish when appended to a command?

explanation.correct: 2>&1 redirects file descriptor 2 (stderr) to wherever file descriptor 1 (stdout) is currently pointing, merging error and normal output into a single stream.
explanation.incorrect: It is not related to a literal filename '1', it does not touch standard input, and by itself it does not perform any appending to a file.
explanation.examTip: Order matters: 'cmd > file 2>&1' merges both streams into file; 'cmd 2>&1 > file' does not merge them the same way.

options.text: Redirects standard output to a file named 1
Redirects standard error to the same destination as standard output
Redirects standard input from file descriptor 2
Appends standard output to file descriptor 1

questions.questionText: Which symbol appends command output to the end of an existing file, rather than overwriting it?

explanation.correct: >> appends output to a file, preserving existing content, while a single > truncates and overwrites the file.
explanation.incorrect: | pipes output into another command, and < redirects a file's content into a command's standard input.
explanation.examTip: One > = overwrite (danger!). Two >> = append (safe, adds to the end).

questions.questionText: Which grep option performs a case-insensitive search?

explanation.correct: grep -i ignores case when matching the search pattern against lines of input.
explanation.incorrect: -v inverts the match (shows non-matching lines), -c prints only a count of matching lines, and -n prefixes matching lines with their line number.
explanation.examTip: grep flags to remember: -i ignore case, -v invert, -n line numbers, -c count, -r recursive.

questions.questionText: In awk, which built-in variable represents the last (Nth) field of the current line?

explanation.correct: $NF refers to the value of the last field on the current line, since NF holds the total number of fields.
explanation.incorrect: $0 represents the entire current line, $1 is the first field, and $FS is the field separator variable, not a field reference.
explanation.examTip: $0 = whole line, $1..$N = individual fields, $NF = last field (NF = 'Number of Fields').

questions.questionText: Which command creates a compressed tar archive named backup.tar.gz from the contents of the /data directory?

explanation.correct: tar -cvzf creates (c) a new archive, shows progress (v), compresses with gzip (z), and writes to the named file (f).
explanation.incorrect: -x extracts an existing archive rather than creating one, -t lists archive contents without extracting, and plain gzip cannot bundle a directory tree into a single tar archive on its own.
explanation.examTip: Mnemonic for tar flags: 'create' c, 'extract' x, 'view/list' t, always paired with 'z' for gzip and 'f' for filename.

questions.questionText: Which command shows a continuously updating, interactive view of running processes and system resource usage?

explanation.correct: top provides a live, auto-refreshing view of processes along with CPU and memory usage.
explanation.incorrect: ps aux gives a static one-time snapshot, jobs lists background/suspended jobs of the current shell, and nohup runs a command immune to hangups (it isn't a monitoring tool).
explanation.examTip: ps = snapshot (one look). top = live dashboard (continuously refreshing) — htop is a friendlier alternative to top.

questions.questionText: Which key combination sends a running foreground process to the background as a suspended job?

explanation.correct: Ctrl+Z suspends the current foreground job, after which 'bg' can resume it running in the background.
explanation.incorrect: Ctrl+C sends SIGINT to terminate a process, Ctrl+D signals end-of-input (EOF), and Ctrl+A moves the cursor to the start of the line in many shells.
explanation.examTip: Ctrl+Z = pause and background. Ctrl+C = kill. Very different results — mixing them up can lose unsaved work.

questions.questionText: Which crontab schedule expression runs a job at 2:30 AM every day?

explanation.correct: Cron fields are 'minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week', so '30 2 * * *' means minute 30, hour 2, every day, every month, every weekday.
explanation.incorrect: '2 30 * * *' swaps minute and hour (would mean 30:02, invalid), '*/30 2 * * *' runs every 30 minutes during hour 2, and '30 2 * * 1' restricts the job to Mondays only.
explanation.examTip: Cron field order: minute-hour-day(month)-month-day(week). Say it as 'm h dom mon dow'.

questions.scenarioText: A junior sysadmin at Initech has just provisioned a fresh Ubuntu server and needs to install the Nginx web server.
questions.questionText: Which command installs a package on a Debian or Ubuntu system using the high-level package manager?

explanation.correct: apt is the high-level package manager for Debian/Ubuntu systems and handles dependency resolution automatically.
explanation.incorrect: yum/dnf are used on Red Hat-family systems, rpm is a low-level installer without automatic dependency resolution, and pacman is Arch Linux's package manager.
explanation.examTip: High-level with dependency resolution: apt (Debian), dnf/yum (Red Hat), pacman (Arch). Low-level, no dependency solving: dpkg, rpm.

metadata.examObjective: 3.8 Debian and Red Hat Package Management

questions.questionText: Which sed command replaces the first occurrence of 'error' with 'warning' on each line of a file?

explanation.correct: sed 's/error/warning/' substitutes only the first match of 'error' on each line with 'warning'.
explanation.incorrect: Adding the g flag would replace every occurrence per line (global), not just the first, and the other two options use invalid sed syntax.
explanation.examTip: sed 's/old/new/' = first match per line. sed 's/old/new/g' = every match per line (g = global).

questions.scenarioText: An engineer at Globex Corp needs to kick off a two-hour data migration script over SSH and then safely disconnect without killing the job.
questions.questionText: A command was run with 'nohup long_task.sh &'. What is the primary effect of nohup in this context?

explanation.correct: nohup ('no hang up') makes a process ignore the SIGHUP signal, so it keeps running even after the terminal that launched it is closed.
explanation.incorrect: nohup does not grant elevated privileges (sudo does), does not schedule future execution (at/cron do), and does not change CPU scheduling priority (nice/renice do).
explanation.examTip: nohup + & is the classic combo for launching a long job that survives logging out of the terminal.

options.text: It runs the script with elevated (root) privileges
It prevents the process from being terminated when the terminal session closes
It schedules the script to run at a later time
It limits the CPU priority of the process

questions.questionText: Which TWO of the following are valid ways to run a command using command substitution?

explanation.correct: Both $(command) (modern, preferred) and `command` (backticks, legacy) perform command substitution, inserting the command's output into the surrounding text.
explanation.incorrect: Curly braces {} are used for brace expansion (generating strings), not command substitution, and %command% is not valid bash syntax.
explanation.examTip: $() is preferred over backticks because it nests cleanly, e.g. $(echo $(date)) — nested backticks require awkward escaping.

questions.questionText: Which TWO redirection operators send a command's output to a file (as opposed to reading input from a file)?

explanation.correct: > overwrites a file with output, and >> appends output to the end of a file — both write data out.
explanation.incorrect: < reads input into a command from a file, and while 2> does write output, it specifically writes stderr; the question is about the general output-writing operators covered here, of which > and >> are the two purely output-writing ones being tested.
explanation.examTip: Arrows point the direction data flows: > and >> point data OUT to a file; < pulls data IN from a file.

questions.questionText: Which TWO of the following are valid quoting mechanisms in bash for controlling variable expansion?

explanation.correct: Single quotes suppress all expansion so variables are treated literally, while double quotes still allow variable and command substitution to occur inside them.
explanation.incorrect: Curly braces are used for brace expansion or variable disambiguation (${VAR}), and parentheses launch a subshell — neither is primarily a quoting mechanism.
explanation.examTip: '$VAR' inside single quotes prints literally as $VAR. "$VAR" inside double quotes expands to the variable's value.

questions.questionText: Which TWO commands can be used to terminate a running process by name rather than by PID?

explanation.correct: killall and pkill both accept a process name and signal all matching processes, without requiring you to look up a PID first.
explanation.incorrect: kill requires a specific numeric PID (not a name), and nice adjusts a process's scheduling priority rather than terminating it.
explanation.examTip: kill needs a PID. killall and pkill work by process NAME — handy when you don't know (or don't want to look up) the PID.

questions.questionText: Which TWO glob patterns would match the filename 'report2.txt'?

explanation.correct: report?.txt matches any single character in place of ?, and report[0-9].txt matches any single digit — both match 'report2.txt'.
explanation.incorrect: report[a-z].txt only matches a lowercase letter in that position (not a digit), and report.txt has no wildcard so it only matches that exact literal filename.
explanation.examTip: ? = exactly one character. [set] = one character from the set. * = zero or more characters.

questions.questionText: Which TWO commands can be used to extract or upgrade individual Debian .deb packages at a low level, without automatic dependency resolution?

explanation.correct: dpkg -i installs a local .deb package file directly, and dpkg -r removes an installed package — both operate at the low level without resolving dependencies automatically.
explanation.incorrect: apt install can also install a local file and does resolve dependencies (making it higher-level), and apt update merely refreshes package indexes rather than installing or removing software.
explanation.examTip: dpkg = low-level, single package, no dependency solving. apt = high-level, handles dependencies automatically.

explanation.incorrect: unset does not just hide a variable — it deletes it entirely, and referencing it afterward returns nothing.
explanation.examTip: unset well and truly deletes; there's no 'undo' short of re-setting the variable's value again.

questions.questionText: Evaluate each statement about pipes and redirection as Yes or No.

explanation.correct: Pipes connect stdout of one process to stdin of the next; /dev/null is a special device that discards anything written to it; tee is specifically designed to do both — write to a file AND pass the data through to standard output at the same time.
explanation.incorrect: tee's whole purpose is splitting output to both the screen and a file simultaneously, unlike a plain redirect which only goes to the file.
explanation.examTip: tee = 'T-splitter' for output: one stream in, two streams out (screen + file).

questions.questionText: Evaluate each statement about grep, sed, and awk as Yes or No.

explanation.correct: grep -r recurses into subdirectories when searching; without -i, sed by default only prints the modified result to standard output and leaves the original file untouched — -i is required to edit the file in place; awk's field variables like $1 and $NF let you print or process specific columns.
explanation.incorrect: Without -i, sed is non-destructive: the source file is unchanged unless you redirect output or explicitly request in-place editing.
explanation.examTip: sed -i = 'in-place' edit (modifies the file). Without -i, sed only writes its result to stdout.

questions.questionText: Evaluate each statement about tar and compression as Yes or No.

explanation.correct: tar -xvzf extracts (x), shows progress (v), decompresses gzip (z), from the named file (f); gzip only compresses a single file/stream and cannot itself bundle multiple files — that bundling job belongs to tar; .tar.gz and .tgz are simply two common naming conventions for the same type of archive.
explanation.incorrect: gzip alone has no concept of multiple files or directory structure — that's specifically what tar provides before gzip compresses the result.
explanation.examTip: tar bundles (multiple files -> one file), gzip compresses (shrinks size). tar -z combines both in one command.

statements.text: tar -xvzf archive.tar.gz extracts a gzip-compressed tar archive.
gzip compression, unlike tar, can bundle multiple files and directories into a single archive.
The .tar.gz and .tgz file extensions both commonly refer to a gzip-compressed tar archive.

questions.questionText: Evaluate each statement about job control as Yes or No.

explanation.correct: & backgrounds a command so you get your prompt back right away; fg resumes a background/suspended job in the foreground; jobs only lists jobs associated with the current shell session, not the whole system (use ps or top for that).
explanation.incorrect: jobs is scoped to the current shell session only — it will not show processes started in other terminals.
explanation.examTip: jobs = current shell's background jobs only. ps aux/top = every process on the whole system.

questions.scenarioText: A system administrator at Umbrella Corp is running low on disk space and needs to archive old, large log files before deleting them.
questions.questionText: A system administrator at Umbrella Corp needs to find all '.log' files larger than 50MB under /var/log and archive them. Arrange the workflow in the correct order.

explanation.correct: You must first identify the target files with find, capture that list, bundle and compress them with tar -czf, and finally confirm the archive was built correctly with tar -tvf.
explanation.incorrect: Attempting to archive before identifying which files match, or skipping verification, risks silently missing files or producing a broken archive.
explanation.examTip: find to discover -> tar -c to create -> tar -t to verify. Verification is an easy step to forget on the exam.

Redirect the list of matching filenames into a text file using >
Create a compressed tar archive of those files with tar -czf
Verify the archive contents with tar -tvf

questions.questionText: Arrange the steps to schedule a script to run automatically every weekday at 6:00 AM using cron.

explanation.correct: crontab -e opens the editor, the cron line schedules the job for 6:00 AM Monday through Friday (1-5), saving commits the change, and crontab -l lists the crontab to confirm it was saved correctly.
explanation.incorrect: Skipping crontab -e (there is no other direct way to add a per-user cron job) or forgetting to verify with crontab -l risks an unsaved or malformed entry going unnoticed.
explanation.examTip: Day-of-week numbering in cron: 0 and 7 both mean Sunday, 1-5 is Monday through Friday.

Add the line: 0 6 * * 1-5 /home/user/backup.sh
Save and exit the editor

questions.scenarioText: A support engineer at Wayne Enterprises notices a background job named 'stuck_worker' consuming excessive CPU and needs to stop it safely.
questions.questionText: Arrange the steps to safely stop a misbehaving background process identified only by name, 'stuck_worker'.

explanation.correct: Best practice is to first identify the PID, attempt a graceful kill (SIGTERM) which allows cleanup, verify whether it worked, and only escalate to kill -9 (SIGKILL) if the process refuses to stop.
explanation.incorrect: Jumping straight to kill -9 skips the graceful shutdown a process may need to release resources or save state cleanly.
explanation.examTip: kill sends SIGTERM by default (polite, can be caught/ignored). kill -9 sends SIGKILL (forceful, cannot be caught).

orderItems.text: Run ps aux | grep stuck_worker to find the process and its PID
Send a graceful termination signal with kill <PID>
Check again with ps aux | grep stuck_worker to see if it stopped
If it is still running, force-terminate it with kill -9 <PID>

questions.questionText: Sort each command into the category describing what it primarily does.

explanation.correct: grep and sed both filter or transform text streams, while kill and nice both act on running processes (terminating one, adjusting the scheduling priority of the other).
explanation.incorrect: sed can look similar to a process command because of its terse syntax, but it operates purely on text streams, not on running processes.
explanation.examTip: Text tools: grep, sed, awk, cut, tr. Process tools: ps, kill, nice, renice, top.

questions.questionText: Sort each redirection symbol into the category describing its direction of data flow.

explanation.correct: > and >> both write shell output out to a file (overwrite vs. append), while < and << (here-document) both bring data in as input to a command.
explanation.incorrect: It is easy to assume >> behaves differently in direction from >, but both point the same way — out to a file — they only differ in overwrite vs. append behavior.
explanation.examTip: The arrow always shows the direction: > and >> point right (out to file); < points left (in from file/source).

questions.questionText: Sort each package management command into the correct package manager family.

explanation.correct: apt and dpkg belong to the Debian/Ubuntu ecosystem (managing .deb packages), while dnf and rpm belong to the Fedora/RHEL ecosystem (managing .rpm packages).
explanation.incorrect: Mixing up which low-level tool (dpkg vs rpm) pairs with which high-level tool (apt vs dnf) is a very common exam mistake.
explanation.examTip: Debian pair: apt (high-level) + dpkg (low-level). Red Hat pair: dnf/yum (high-level) + rpm (low-level).

questions.questionText: Which firmware interface is the modern replacement for legacy BIOS, offering faster boot and support for larger disks?

explanation.correct: UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) is the modern firmware standard that replaced legacy BIOS, supporting faster boot and GPT disks larger than 2TB.
explanation.incorrect: GRUB is a bootloader (software that loads the kernel, run by BIOS/UEFI), initramfs is a temporary root filesystem used during boot, and systemd is an init system, not firmware.
explanation.examTip: Firmware first (BIOS/UEFI) -> bootloader (GRUB) -> kernel + initramfs -> init system (systemd).

questions.questionText: Which command is used to view, start, stop, enable, or disable services under systemd?

explanation.correct: systemctl is the primary command-line tool for managing systemd units, including services.
explanation.incorrect: service is a legacy SysVinit-compatible wrapper, chkconfig manages SysVinit runlevel links, and initctl is associated with the Upstart init system.
explanation.examTip: systemctl start|stop|restart|enable|disable|status <service> — the core systemd service management syntax.

questions.scenarioText: An operations engineer at Wonka Industries needs to review recent boot and service logs after a server unexpectedly restarted overnight.
questions.questionText: Which command displays and allows filtering of the systemd journal logs?

explanation.correct: journalctl reads and filters the systemd journal, which centralizes logs from services, the kernel, and boot messages.
explanation.incorrect: dmesg shows only kernel ring buffer messages, syslog is a logging protocol/daemon name rather than a viewing command, and logger is used to add entries to the log rather than view them.
explanation.examTip: journalctl -u <service> filters logs for one specific systemd unit — extremely useful for troubleshooting a failing service.

questions.questionText: Which command lists information about a system's block devices, such as disks and partitions?

explanation.correct: lsblk lists block devices in a tree view, showing disks, partitions, and their mount points.
explanation.incorrect: lscpu reports CPU architecture details, lsusb lists connected USB devices, and lspci lists PCI devices such as network and graphics cards.
explanation.examTip: The 'ls' family: lsblk=block devices, lscpu=CPU info, lspci=PCI devices, lsusb=USB devices.

questions.questionText: Which command shows disk space usage for mounted filesystems in a human-readable format?

explanation.correct: df -h reports free and used space on mounted filesystems, with sizes shown in human-readable units (K, M, G).
explanation.incorrect: du -h reports the disk usage of files/directories (not overall filesystem space), free -h reports memory usage, and mount -h simply prints mount's help text.
explanation.examTip: df = Disk Filesystem (space per mounted volume). du = Disk Usage (space consumed by files/folders).

questions.questionText: Which file defines filesystems that should be automatically mounted at boot time?

explanation.correct: /etc/fstab (filesystem table) lists filesystems, their mount points, types, and options to be mounted automatically at boot.
explanation.incorrect: /etc/mtab and /proc/mounts reflect currently mounted filesystems (a runtime record), not the configuration of what should be mounted, and /etc/mounts is not a standard file.
explanation.examTip: fstab = Filesystem TABle, the boot-time mount configuration. mtab/proc/mounts just reflect current state.

questions.questionText: Which command sends ICMP echo requests to test network reachability of a host?

explanation.correct: ping sends ICMP echo request packets to a host and reports whether/how quickly it responds.
explanation.incorrect: traceroute maps the path packets take across multiple hops, dig queries DNS records, and ss displays socket statistics rather than testing reachability.
explanation.examTip: ping = 'is it alive?' traceroute = 'what path does it take to get there?'

questions.questionText: Which command displays and can modify the current system date, time, and timezone under systemd?

explanation.correct: timedatectl is the systemd tool for viewing and setting the system clock, timezone, and NTP synchronization status.
explanation.incorrect: date only displays or sets the current date/time string (not timezone/NTP settings), hwclock reads/writes the hardware clock specifically, and tzselect is an interactive tool for choosing a timezone (older, non-systemd approach).
explanation.examTip: timedatectl is the modern, systemd-native, all-in-one tool for date, time, timezone, and NTP settings.

questions.questionText: Which command queries a DNS server to resolve a domain name to its IP address, providing detailed record information?

explanation.correct: dig (Domain Information Groper) sends DNS queries and returns detailed information about DNS records, such as A, MX, or NS records.
explanation.incorrect: hostname reports or sets the local machine's hostname (not DNS lookups), ip addr shows the local machine's own network interfaces, and ss reports active socket/connection statistics.
explanation.examTip: dig and nslookup both query DNS; dig gives more detailed, script-friendly output and is generally preferred today.

questions.questionText: Which /proc file provides real-time information about installed CPU details, such as model name and core count?

explanation.correct: /proc/cpuinfo is a virtual file exposing detailed information about each processor core recognized by the kernel.
explanation.incorrect: /proc/meminfo reports memory statistics instead, /proc/version reports the running kernel version string, and /proc/mounts lists currently mounted filesystems.
explanation.examTip: /proc is a virtual filesystem — files there don't exist on disk, they're generated live by the kernel on each read.

questions.questionText: During the Linux boot process, what is the primary purpose of the initramfs (initial RAM filesystem)?

explanation.correct: initramfs is a small, temporary filesystem loaded into RAM that contains the drivers and tools needed to locate and mount the real root filesystem before the boot process hands off control to it.
explanation.incorrect: It is not used for permanent user storage, it does not replace a bootloader like GRUB (which loads the kernel and initramfs in the first place), and it is unrelated to swap space.
explanation.examTip: initramfs exists so the kernel can load storage/filesystem drivers (e.g. for RAID or encrypted disks) before it can even see the real root filesystem.

options.text: It permanently stores all user files during normal operation
It provides a temporary root filesystem with drivers needed to mount the real root filesystem
It replaces the need for a bootloader entirely
It stores swap space used when physical RAM is exhausted

questions.questionText: Which TWO of the following are valid systemctl subcommands for managing a service?

explanation.correct: systemctl enable configures a service to start automatically at boot, and systemctl status reports whether a service is currently running along with recent log output.
explanation.incorrect: install and compile are not systemctl subcommands for managing services; systemd deals with pre-defined unit files rather than compiling or installing software.
explanation.examTip: Common systemctl verbs: start, stop, restart, reload, enable, disable, status, is-active, is-enabled.

questions.questionText: Which TWO filesystem types are commonly supported natively on modern Linux distributions?

explanation.correct: ext4 and xfs are both native Linux filesystems with full, built-in read/write support on essentially all modern distributions.
explanation.incorrect: NTFS write support historically required extra drivers/utilities (not enabled 'by default' on many systems in the way described), and APFS is Apple's proprietary filesystem, not natively supported by the Linux kernel.
explanation.examTip: Native Linux filesystems: ext4, xfs, btrfs. Foreign filesystems (Windows/macOS) need extra drivers: ntfs-3g, apfs-fuse.

questions.questionText: Which TWO commands can be used to display information about the system's network interfaces and their assigned IP addresses?

explanation.correct: ip addr (the modern tool) and ifconfig (the older, sometimes deprecated tool) both display network interface configuration, including assigned IP addresses.
explanation.incorrect: ping tests reachability of a remote host rather than showing local interface configuration, and dig performs DNS lookups.
explanation.examTip: ip is the modern replacement for the older, sometimes-unavailable-by-default ifconfig — know both for the exam.

questions.questionText: Which TWO commands can be used to check whether a remote host or port is reachable over the network?

explanation.correct: ping tests basic reachability with ICMP echo requests, and traceroute reveals reachability along with each hop the packets pass through.
explanation.incorrect: ss reports information about local sockets/connections already established (not testing new reachability), and hwclock manages the hardware clock, unrelated to networking.
explanation.examTip: For reachability testing: ping (simple) and traceroute (hop-by-hop path) are the two classic tools.

questions.questionText: Which TWO of the following are valid systemd unit states reported by 'systemctl is-enabled'?

explanation.correct: systemctl is-enabled reports whether a unit is configured to start at boot, with typical results including 'enabled' and 'disabled' (among a few others like 'static' or 'masked').
explanation.incorrect: 'compiled' and 'archived' are not systemd unit states; systemd deals with unit configuration files, not compilation or archiving.
explanation.examTip: is-enabled answers 'will this start at boot?' while is-active answers 'is this running right now?' — two different questions.

questions.questionText: Evaluate each statement about the Linux boot process as Yes or No.

explanation.correct: GRUB (GRand Unified Bootloader) loads the kernel; systemd is indeed the default init system on most mainstream distributions today (Ubuntu, Fedora, RHEL, Debian, etc.); runlevels actually originated with SysVinit — systemd uses the analogous concept of 'targets' instead.
explanation.incorrect: Runlevels predate systemd; systemd's rough equivalent concept is called a 'target' (e.g. multi-user.target corresponds to runlevel 3).
explanation.examTip: SysVinit = runlevels (0-6). systemd = targets (e.g., graphical.target, multi-user.target).

statements.text: GRUB is a bootloader responsible for loading the Linux kernel into memory.

questions.questionText: Evaluate each statement about hardware inspection commands as Yes or No.

explanation.correct: lspci reports PCI-connected hardware; dmesg is a key troubleshooting tool for kernel and driver messages, especially around boot and hardware detection; lsusb specifically lists USB devices, not filesystems (that's df/mount's job).
explanation.incorrect: lsusb lists USB devices, not mounted filesystems — that distinction is a common source of exam confusion with similarly-named commands.
explanation.examTip: The ls-prefixed hardware commands (lspci, lsusb, lsblk, lscpu) each inspect one specific hardware category.

statements.text: lspci lists devices connected to the PCI bus, such as network and graphics cards.
dmesg displays messages from the kernel ring buffer, useful for diagnosing hardware and driver issues.
lsusb is used to list mounted filesystems rather than connected USB devices.

questions.questionText: Evaluate each statement about disks and filesystems as Yes or No.

explanation.correct: mount attaches a filesystem at a mount point directory; fsck actually checks and repairs an existing filesystem for errors (mkfs is the tool used to format/create a new filesystem); the system reads /etc/fstab during boot to determine what to automatically mount.
explanation.incorrect: mkfs creates a filesystem; fsck checks and repairs one that already exists — an easy pair to mix up.
explanation.examTip: mkfs = 'make filesystem' (formatting). fsck = 'filesystem check' (repair, run after unclean shutdowns).

statements.text: The mount command attaches a filesystem to a directory (mount point) so its contents become accessible.
fsck is used to format a new filesystem onto a partition before it can be used.
/etc/fstab entries are automatically processed by the system at boot time to mount listed filesystems.

questions.questionText: Evaluate each statement about networking configuration as Yes or No.

explanation.correct: /etc/hosts provides local, static hostname-to-IP mappings checked before DNS in most default configurations; NetworkManager manages both wired and wireless (Wi-Fi) connections, among other network types; /etc/resolv.conf traditionally lists nameserver entries used for DNS resolution.
explanation.incorrect: NetworkManager is a general-purpose network configuration service covering Ethernet, Wi-Fi, VPNs, and more — not limited to wired connections.
explanation.examTip: /etc/hosts is checked before DNS by default on most systems — great for quick local overrides during testing.

statements.text: The /etc/hosts file allows manual mapping of hostnames to IP addresses without querying DNS.
NetworkManager is a service exclusively used for managing wired Ethernet connections and cannot manage Wi-Fi.
The /etc/resolv.conf file traditionally specifies which DNS servers a system should query.

questions.questionText: Complete each statement about systemd by choosing the correct command from its dropdown.

explanation.correct: systemctl enable configures a service to launch at boot (it does not start it immediately, unlike systemctl start), and journalctl -u filters the systemd journal to a specific unit.
explanation.incorrect: systemctl start only starts the service for the current session without persisting across reboots, and dmesg only shows kernel messages, not per-service application logs.
explanation.examTip: enable = start at boot (persistent). start = start right now (one-time, until reboot). Use both together for immediate + persistent effect.

questions.questionText: Arrange the high-level stages of a typical Linux boot process in the correct order.

explanation.correct: This reflects the standard boot sequence: firmware hands off to the bootloader, which loads the kernel, which then hands off to the init system to bring up userspace services.
explanation.incorrect: Any other ordering, such as starting services before the kernel has mounted the root filesystem, is not physically possible in this sequence.
explanation.examTip: Firmware -> Bootloader -> Kernel -> Init system — the four-stage boot chain every Linux system follows.

questions.questionText: A sysadmin at Stark Industries needs to add a new disk, create a filesystem on it, and mount it persistently. Arrange the correct workflow.

explanation.correct: You must first identify the correct device, format it with a filesystem, register it for persistent mounting in /etc/fstab, and then apply that configuration immediately with mount -a rather than waiting for a reboot.
explanation.incorrect: Editing /etc/fstab before creating a filesystem, or mounting before formatting, would result in errors since there is no valid filesystem yet to mount.
explanation.examTip: mount -a reads /etc/fstab and mounts everything listed there that isn't already mounted — a quick way to test fstab changes without rebooting.

Mount all fstab entries immediately with mount -a

questions.scenarioText: An operations engineer at Wonka Industries discovers that the 'webapp' systemd service is not running after a recent deployment.
questions.questionText: Arrange the steps to diagnose why a systemd service named 'webapp' failed to start.

explanation.correct: A logical troubleshooting flow starts with a quick status check, moves to the detailed journal for more context, identifies the root cause from the logs, and finally applies a fix and restarts the service to confirm resolution.
explanation.incorrect: Restarting the service before investigating the logs would likely reproduce the same failure without revealing why it happened.
explanation.examTip: systemctl status gives a quick summary; journalctl -u gives the deep, scrollable history — use both together when debugging.

orderItems.text: Run systemctl status webapp to see the current state and recent log lines
Run journalctl -u webapp for the full, detailed log history of the service
Identify the specific error message in the logs
Correct the underlying issue and run systemctl restart webapp

questions.questionText: Sort each command into the category describing what it primarily reports on.

explanation.correct: lscpu and lspci report on installed hardware (CPU and PCI devices respectively), while df and du report on disk space usage at the filesystem and file/directory level respectively.
explanation.incorrect: It's easy to lump all 'ls'-prefixed commands together, but lsblk (block devices) sits closer to the disk-usage group conceptually even though it's not one of the two listed disk commands here.
explanation.examTip: Hardware discovery commands start with ls (lscpu, lspci, lsusb, lsblk); disk space commands are df and du.

questions.questionText: Sort each item into the correct init system category.

explanation.correct: Runlevels and /etc/init.d scripts are core concepts of the older SysVinit system, while targets and unit files are the equivalent concepts used by the modern systemd init system.
explanation.incorrect: Confusing 'runlevels' with 'targets' is common since they serve a similar conceptual purpose but belong to different init systems entirely.
explanation.examTip: SysVinit: runlevels + init.d scripts. systemd: targets + unit files. Different generations, similar goals.

questions.questionText: In the ls -l output '-rwxr-xr--', what permission does the file's group have?

explanation.correct: The middle triplet 'r-x' shows the group has read and execute permission, but not write.
explanation.incorrect: The first triplet (rwx) is the owner's permissions, and the final triplet (r--) is 'others', which here has read-only access.
explanation.examTip: Positions in ls -l: [type][owner rwx][group rwx][other rwx] — always read left to right in that order.

metadata.examObjective: 5.1 Basic Security and Identifying User Types

questions.questionText: What octal value represents read, write, and execute permissions combined?

explanation.correct: Read (4) + write (2) + execute (1) = 7, which represents full rwx permission.
explanation.incorrect: 4 alone is read-only, 5 is read+execute, and 6 is read+write without execute.
explanation.examTip: Memorize: r=4, w=2, x=1. Add them for each of owner/group/other to build the three-digit octal number.

questions.questionText: Which chmod command grants execute permission to the owner of a file, leaving all other permissions unchanged?

explanation.correct: chmod u+x adds execute permission specifically for the user/owner (u), without touching group or other permissions.
explanation.incorrect: o+x targets 'others' rather than the owner, a+x targets all three categories, and chmod 111 sets an absolute octal value (execute-only for everyone), which overwrites all existing permissions rather than adding to them.
explanation.examTip: Symbolic chmod is additive/subtractive (+/-) and only touches the specified category; octal chmod always sets the ENTIRE permission set from scratch.

questions.questionText: Which octal permission corresponds to the symbolic notation 'rw-r--r--'?

explanation.correct: rw- (6) for owner, r-- (4) for group, and r-- (4) for other combine to 644, a very common default permission for regular files.
explanation.incorrect: 600 would be rw------- (owner only), 664 would give the group write access too (rw-rw-r--), and 744 would give the owner execute permission as well (rwxr--r--).
explanation.examTip: 644 is the classic 'default file' permission: owner can read/write, everyone else can only read.

questions.questionText: A file has the SUID bit set and permissions rwsr-xr-x. What effect does the SUID bit have when the file is executed?

explanation.correct: SUID (Set User ID) causes an executable to run with the permissions of the file's owner, not the invoking user — classically used by programs like passwd that need elevated access briefly.
explanation.incorrect: SUID does not restrict execution to root, has nothing to do with encryption, and does not affect write/modify permissions for the group (that would be the ordinary group-write bit, not SUID).
explanation.examTip: SUID shows as 's' in the owner's execute position (rws); if the owner lacked execute permission it would show as capital 'S' instead.

questions.questionText: What is the primary purpose of the sticky bit when set on a shared, world-writable directory like /tmp?

explanation.correct: The sticky bit on a directory restricts deletion/renaming so that only the file's owner (or root) can remove it, even if other users have write access to the directory itself — exactly how /tmp stays usable by everyone without users deleting each other's files.
explanation.incorrect: The sticky bit does not block file creation, does not control group inheritance (that is SGID's role), and has no relation to compression.
explanation.examTip: Sticky bit shows as 't' (or 'T' if others lack execute) in the 'other' execute position of ls -l, e.g. drwxrwxrwt for /tmp.

questions.questionText: If a user's umask is set to 022, what will the resulting default permissions be for a newly created file (starting from a base of 666)?

explanation.correct: 666 (base for files) minus the umask 022 removes write permission for group and other, resulting in 644 (rw-r--r--).
explanation.incorrect: 600 would result from a umask of 066, and 755 is the typical result for directories (base 777) with a 022 umask, not files.
explanation.examTip: umask SUBTRACTS permissions from the base. Files start at 666, directories start at 777 — umask 022 is extremely common as a default.

questions.questionText: Which command changes both the owner and group of a file in a single invocation?

explanation.correct: chown accepts the syntax 'user:group' to change both the owning user and the owning group of a file in one command.
explanation.incorrect: chmod only changes permission bits (not ownership), chgrp only changes the group, and usermod modifies user account properties, not file ownership.
explanation.examTip: chown user:group file — the colon syntax updates owner AND group together; chgrp alone only touches the group.

questions.scenarioText: A security auditor at Stark Industries is reviewing where user password data is stored on a Linux server as part of a compliance check.
questions.questionText: Which file traditionally stores the hashed passwords for local user accounts, separate from basic account information?

explanation.correct: /etc/shadow stores hashed passwords and password aging information, and is readable only by root for security.
explanation.incorrect: /etc/passwd stores basic account info (username, UID, home directory, shell) but no longer stores actual password hashes on modern systems, /etc/group defines group memberships, and /etc/security is not a standard single file in this context.
explanation.examTip: /etc/passwd is world-readable (usernames aren't secret); /etc/shadow is root-only readable (password hashes must stay protected).

questions.questionText: Which command creates a new user account on most Linux distributions?

explanation.correct: useradd creates a new user account with the specified options, such as home directory and shell.
explanation.incorrect: usermod modifies an existing account, userdel removes one, and passwd sets or changes a password for an existing account.
explanation.examTip: add/mod/del pattern applies to both users and groups: useradd/usermod/userdel and groupadd/groupmod/groupdel.

questions.questionText: Which command displays a user's numeric user ID (UID), group ID (GID), and all group memberships?

explanation.correct: id displays the UID, primary GID, and all supplementary group memberships for a user in one combined output.
explanation.incorrect: whoami only prints the current username, groups alone lists group names without numeric IDs, and who shows currently logged-in users on the system.
explanation.examTip: id gives you everything at once: UID, GID, and groups — whoami and groups each only show a subset.

questions.questionText: Which command should be used to safely edit the /etc/sudoers file, providing syntax checking before saving?

explanation.correct: visudo locks the sudoers file, opens it in an editor, and validates the syntax before saving, preventing a malformed file from locking out sudo access entirely.
explanation.incorrect: Editing /etc/sudoers directly with vi or nano skips this safety check, risking a broken file that could lock out all sudo users, and sudoedit /etc/passwd edits the wrong file entirely for this purpose.
explanation.examTip: Always use visudo for sudoers — a syntax error saved directly with a plain editor can lock every admin out of sudo.

questions.questionText: Which command switches to another user account and loads that user's full login environment, including their home directory and shell profile?

explanation.correct: su - username (or su -l username) starts a login shell as the target user, loading their environment variables and changing to their home directory.
explanation.incorrect: su username (without the dash) switches user but keeps the invoking user's existing environment, sudo username is not valid syntax for switching users in this way, and chsh changes a user's default login shell rather than switching sessions.
explanation.examTip: su alone keeps your old environment; su - simulates a fresh login as that user, with their PATH, HOME, and profile.

questions.questionText: In an SSH key pair used for authentication, which key should be placed in the ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file on the remote server?

explanation.correct: The public key is safe to share and is placed in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server to permit login using the matching private key.
explanation.incorrect: The private key must never be shared or placed on a remote server, combining both keys is not how SSH key authentication works, and known_hosts stores fingerprints of servers you've connected to, not authentication keys.
explanation.examTip: Public key -> goes on the SERVER (authorized_keys). Private key -> stays on your LOCAL machine, never shared.

questions.questionText: Which sshd_config directive, when set to 'no', disables the ability to log in via SSH using a password (allowing key-based authentication only)?

explanation.correct: Setting PasswordAuthentication no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config disables password-based logins, forcing users to authenticate with SSH keys instead — a strong security hardening step.
explanation.incorrect: PermitRootLogin controls whether the root account specifically can log in via SSH, Port is not a yes/no directive (it specifies a port number), and setting PubkeyAuthentication to no would disable key-based login instead, the opposite of the intended hardening.
explanation.examTip: Hardening SSH commonly means: PasswordAuthentication no + PermitRootLogin no, forcing key-based, non-root logins.

questions.scenarioText: A sysadmin at Gringotts Bank is hardening a newly deployed server and needs remote administrators to still be able to reach it over SSH.
questions.questionText: Which ufw command allows incoming traffic on port 22 (SSH)?

explanation.correct: ufw allow 22 opens port 22 to incoming connections, commonly used to permit SSH access.
explanation.incorrect: ufw deny 22 blocks the port instead, ufw status displays current rules (it does not take a port argument to allow anything), and ufw enable simply turns the firewall on/off globally without specifying a port.
explanation.examTip: ufw = 'Uncomplicated Firewall.' Basic syntax: ufw allow/deny <port or service>, ufw enable/disable, ufw status.

questions.questionText: Which gpg option is used to generate a new public/private key pair?

explanation.correct: gpg --gen-key launches an interactive process to create a new GPG public/private key pair.
explanation.incorrect: --encrypt and --decrypt operate on data using existing keys rather than creating new ones, and --list-keys only displays keys already present in the keyring.
explanation.examTip: gpg workflow: --gen-key creates keys, --encrypt/--decrypt use them, --list-keys inspects what you already have.

questions.questionText: Which best describes symmetric encryption, as opposed to asymmetric encryption?

explanation.correct: Symmetric encryption uses one shared secret key for both encryption and decryption, requiring that key to be securely distributed to all parties beforehand.
explanation.incorrect: A public/private key pair describes asymmetric encryption instead, symmetric encryption works on any binary data (not just text), and it does not inherently require a certificate authority.
explanation.examTip: Symmetric = one shared key (fast, but key distribution is hard). Asymmetric = public/private key pair (slower, solves the distribution problem).

questions.questionText: Which TWO commands can be used to change the group ownership of a file?

explanation.correct: chgrp changes only the group owner of a file, and chown can change the group as well when used with the 'user:group' or ':group' syntax.
explanation.incorrect: chmod only changes permission bits, not ownership, and usermod modifies user account settings rather than file ownership.
explanation.examTip: chown :group file (no username before the colon) changes only the group, functioning the same as chgrp group file.

questions.questionText: Which TWO of the following are valid octal representations of the SUID, SGID, or sticky bit prefix in a 4-digit chmod value?

explanation.correct: A leading 4 sets SUID and a leading 2 sets SGID as the special permission digit in a 4-digit chmod value.
explanation.incorrect: 1755 sets the sticky bit (which is valid on its own, but is not one of the two values being asked about here relative to SUID/SGID), and 0655 sets no special bit at all (0 means none).
explanation.examTip: Special bit digit: 4=SUID, 2=SGID, 1=sticky. They can even combine, e.g. 6755 sets both SUID and SGID.

questions.questionText: Which TWO files are central to Linux local user account management, storing account and password information respectively?

explanation.correct: /etc/passwd stores basic account details (username, UID, GID, home, shell), and /etc/shadow stores the hashed passwords and aging policy for those accounts.
explanation.incorrect: /etc/hosts maps hostnames to IP addresses and is unrelated to user accounts, and /etc/fstab configures filesystem mounts.
explanation.examTip: passwd = account metadata (readable by all). shadow = password hashes (root-only) — a pair you'll be tested on together.

questions.questionText: Which TWO commands can be used to add an existing user to an additional supplementary group?

explanation.correct: usermod -aG appends a user to a supplementary group without removing them from existing groups, and gpasswd -a also adds a user to a group.
explanation.incorrect: groupadd only creates new groups (it does not add existing users to them), and userdel removes user accounts entirely rather than managing group membership.
explanation.examTip: Always use usermod -aG (append), never plain usermod -G, which would REPLACE all existing supplementary group memberships.

questions.questionText: Which TWO of the following sshd_config settings are commonly changed together to harden SSH access on a production server?

explanation.correct: Disabling root login and disabling password authentication (forcing key-based login) are two of the most common, effective SSH hardening measures used together.
explanation.incorrect: Leaving Port at the unchanged default of 22 does not itself harden anything (changing the port is only weak obscurity, not real security), and Protocol 1 is an old, insecure SSH protocol version that should be avoided entirely, not enabled.
explanation.examTip: Root login + password auth are the two biggest attack surfaces for SSH brute-forcing — disable both as a baseline.

questions.questionText: Which TWO commands display current firewall rules or status on a Linux system?

explanation.correct: ufw status reports the current firewall state and active rules, and iptables -L lists the currently loaded iptables rules.
explanation.incorrect: ufw allow adds a new rule rather than displaying existing ones, and iptables -A appends a new rule to a chain instead of listing current rules.
explanation.examTip: -L in iptables = List (view rules). -A = Append (add a new rule). Similar letters, opposite actions.

questions.questionText: Evaluate each statement about the Linux permission model as Yes or No.

explanation.correct: Linux permissions are split into owner/group/other; write permission on a directory itself governs the ability to add/remove entries in it; reading a file's contents with cat only requires read permission, not execute.
explanation.incorrect: Execute permission on a file is needed to run it as a program/script, not to view its contents — that requires read permission instead.
explanation.examTip: Directory permissions work differently than file permissions: write on a directory means 'can add/remove entries', not 'can edit the directory's own content'.

questions.questionText: Evaluate each statement about chmod as Yes or No.

explanation.incorrect: Unlike symbolic +/- notation, octal chmod is absolute — it overwrites the entire permission set every time, regardless of prior permissions.
explanation.examTip: Symbolic (+/-) = relative change. Octal (750, etc.) = absolute, complete replacement of all permission bits.

questions.questionText: Evaluate each statement about special permissions (SUID, SGID, sticky bit) as Yes or No.

explanation.correct: SGID on a directory makes new files inherit the directory's group ownership, useful for shared team directories; most modern Linux kernels intentionally ignore the SUID bit on shell scripts for security reasons, unlike compiled binaries where it works normally; the sticky bit's classic real-world use is exactly on shared, world-writable directories like /tmp.
explanation.incorrect: SUID on shell scripts is ignored by the kernel on most modern systems as a security measure against a well-known class of exploits — it only reliably works on compiled binaries.
explanation.examTip: SGID on a directory = 'inherit my group.' SUID on a script = usually ignored by the kernel for security reasons.

questions.questionText: Evaluate each statement about umask as Yes or No.

explanation.correct: umask subtracts (masks out) bits from the default base permissions; a umask of 000 removes nothing, so new files get the full base permission (666 for files, 777 for directories), the opposite of no access; system-wide umask defaults are commonly set in /etc/profile or /etc/bashrc-style files.
explanation.incorrect: A umask of 000 is the LEAST restrictive setting — it removes no bits at all, granting maximum default permissions, not zero permissions.
explanation.examTip: Higher umask number = more restrictive result. umask 000 = most permissive; umask 077 = very restrictive (owner-only).

questions.questionText: Evaluate each statement about user and group management as Yes or No.

questions.questionText: Evaluate each statement about sudo and privilege escalation as Yes or No.

explanation.correct: The sudoers syntax 'user host=(runas) commands' with all ALL values grants broad access as described; many distributions pre-configure sudo access for members of the wheel (Red Hat-family) or sudo (Debian-family) group; sudo -i starts a full login shell as root with root's environment, unlike a plain sudo command which runs a single command while largely preserving the caller's environment.
explanation.incorrect: sudo -i behaves like logging in fresh as root (new environment), while plain 'sudo command' just elevates privileges for that one command while mostly keeping your existing shell environment.
explanation.examTip: sudoers syntax: user host=(runas_user) commands. 'ALL=(ALL) ALL' is the broadest possible grant.

explanation.correct: ssh-keygen creates a new key pair; ssh-copy-id actually copies your PUBLIC key to the remote server's authorized_keys file, never the private key; known_hosts records host fingerprints seen on prior connections so SSH can warn you if a host's key unexpectedly changes.

questions.questionText: Evaluate each statement about firewalls and encryption basics as Yes or No.

explanation.correct: ufw ('Uncomplicated Firewall') is indeed a simpler front-end over the underlying iptables/netfilter framework; to send someone an asymmetrically encrypted message, you encrypt it with their public key so only their matching private key can decrypt it; symmetric and asymmetric encryption are fundamentally different approaches (shared secret key vs. key pairs), not just a difference in key length.
